item.title: Understanding from Machine Learning Models (2022)
item.author: Emily Sullivan
item.description: Reading guide only; complete published PDF available through OPDS.
item.content:encoded:
Emily Sullivan (2022). Understanding from Machine Learning Models. British Journal for the Philosophy of Science 73(1), 109–133. DOI: 10.1093/bjps/axz035.

Reading guide (not full text)

Sullivan distinguishes understanding a model from understanding a phenomenon through that model. Her account of link uncertainty shifts attention toward the empirical evidence connecting machine learning models to their scientific targets.

Reading question

What kind of evidence would reduce link uncertainty sufficiently for a predictive model to provide explanatory understanding?

Complete published PDF (University of Pittsburgh teaching site). Public redistribution permission not verified; full PDF available through OPDS.

item.title: Climbing towards NLU: On Meaning, Form, and Understanding in the Age of Data (2020)
item.author: Emily M. Bender; Alexander Koller
item.description: Reading guide; complete published PDF available through OPDS.
item.content:encoded:
Emily M. Bender and Alexander Koller (2020). Climbing towards NLU: On Meaning, Form, and Understanding in the Age of Data. ACL 2020, pp. 5185–5198. DOI: 10.18653/v1/2020.acl-main.463.

Reading guide (not full text)

The authors argue that training on linguistic form alone cannot establish meaning, understood through communicative intent. Their thought experiments connect classical debates about computation and understanding with neural language models.

Reading question

Does their definition of meaning presuppose a particular kind of linguistic subject, and how does that affect the impossibility argument?

Complete published PDF (14 pages) | ACL record. ACL materials published since 2016 are licensed CC BY 4.0. Full text is available through OPDS; this RSS entry contains a guide only.

item.title: John R. Searle (1980) - Minds, Brains, and Programs
item.description: Reading guide and full original PDF link; direct PDF download in OPDS.
item.content:encoded:
John R. Searle (1980). Minds, Brains, and Programs. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 3(3), 417–424. DOI: 10.1017/S0140525X00005756.

Why read this paper?

Following Turing's imitation game, Searle's Chinese Room examines whether executing a formal program is sufficient for understanding and intentionality. It provides a foundational challenge for philosophical accounts of language competence in artificial intelligence.

Reading question

Does the Chinese Room establish a general limitation on computational understanding, or does its conclusion depend on how the relevant linguistic subject is individuated?

Reading guide: Download the complete published paper through the OPDS catalog. The university-hosted PDF includes the original target article, subsequent commentaries and Searle's response.

item.title: Alan M. Turing (1950) - Computing Machinery and Intelligence
item.description: Reading guide and links to the original paper.
item.content:encoded:
Alan M. Turing (1950). Computing Machinery and Intelligence. Mind, 59(236), 433–460.

DOI: 10.1093/mind/LIX.236.433.

Why read this paper?

Turing introduces the imitation game as a way of investigating machine intelligence through linguistic behaviour. The paper is an important starting point for debates about the relationship between language use, intelligence and understanding.

Reading question

Does the imitation game take human linguistic performance as a benchmark, and how does that choice shape the inquiry into machine intelligence?

Reading guide only: The original paper is linked below. Its full text has not been republished because permission for redistribution has not been verified.
